title: Opinions & Feelings
subtitle: Say what you think, what you want and what you feel

lessons.title: À mon avis
lessons.description: Express and nuance an opinion with penser, trouver and croire que plus the indicative.

blocks.heading: The three opinion verbs
blocks.body: Penser, croire and trouver are the backbone of French opinions. Penser que introduces a reasoned judgement, croire que a belief you are less sure of, and trouver que a personal impression based on your own experience. All three are followed by que and, in the affirmative, by the indicative — the ordinary tenses you already know.

examples.french: Je pense que ce film est excellent.
examples.english: I think this film is excellent.

examples.french: Je crois qu'il a raison.
examples.english: I believe he is right.
examples.note: que becomes qu' before a vowel

examples.french: Je trouve que la ville a beaucoup changé.
examples.english: I find that the city has changed a lot.

examples.french: Nous pensons que la réunion sera longue.
examples.english: We think the meeting will be long.

examples.french: Elle croit que nous avons oublié son anniversaire.
examples.english: She thinks we forgot her birthday.

examples.french: Tu trouves que j'exagère ?
examples.english: Do you find that I'm exaggerating?

blocks.tip: Never drop que. English says "I think it's true", but French always needs "Je pense que c'est vrai".

blocks.heading: Opinion phrases before the sentence
blocks.body: You can also open with a short phrase and then simply state your view. À mon avis, selon moi and d'après moi all mean "in my opinion", with selon moi sounding slightly more formal. Personnellement and franchement add a personal, honest colour. These phrases are followed by a normal sentence — no que needed.

examples.french: À mon avis, c'est une très bonne idée.
examples.english: In my opinion, it's a very good idea.

examples.french: Selon moi, le problème vient d'ailleurs.
examples.english: In my view, the problem comes from somewhere else.

examples.french: D'après moi, il faut tout recommencer.
examples.english: According to me, we have to start all over again.

examples.french: Personnellement, je préfère rester à la maison.
examples.english: Personally, I prefer to stay at home.

examples.french: Franchement, ce restaurant est décevant.
examples.english: Honestly, this restaurant is disappointing.

examples.french: En ce qui me concerne, la question est réglée.
examples.english: As far as I'm concerned, the matter is settled.

blocks.tip: Avoid saying "à mon opinion" — the fixed phrase is à mon avis.

blocks.heading: Nuance: how sure are you?
blocks.body: French speakers rarely state an opinion flatly; they signal how confident they are. Je suis sûr que and je suis persuadé que are strong; j'ai l'impression que and il me semble que are careful; j'ai tendance à penser que is deliberately soft. Adding plutôt (rather) or un peu (a bit) softens an adjective too.

examples.french: Je suis persuadé que tu vas réussir.
examples.english: I'm convinced that you're going to succeed.

examples.french: J'ai l'impression qu'il ne nous écoute pas.
examples.english: I get the impression he isn't listening to us.

examples.french: J'ai tendance à penser que c'est trop cher.
examples.english: I tend to think it's too expensive.

examples.french: Je trouve ça plutôt réussi.
examples.english: I find that rather successful.

examples.french: Je suis mitigé : le début est lent.
examples.english: I have mixed feelings: the beginning is slow.

examples.french: À vrai dire, je n'en suis pas certain.
examples.english: To tell the truth, I'm not certain about it.

blocks.tip: In a debate, starting with "j'ai l'impression que" makes it easier for the other person to disagree politely.

blocks.heading: Affirmative opinion = indicative
blocks.body: When penser, croire, trouver, être sûr and espérer are affirmative, the speaker presents the idea as real, so French uses the indicative: present, passé composé, imparfait or futur, exactly as in a normal sentence. Do not be tempted to use a subjunctive here — that comes later, and only in specific cases.

examples.french: Je pense qu'il vient ce soir.
examples.english: I think he's coming tonight.

examples.french: Je crois qu'elle est déjà partie.
examples.english: I think she has already left.

examples.french: Nous trouvions que le prix était correct.
examples.english: We thought the price was fair.

examples.french: Je suis sûr que tout ira bien.
examples.english: I'm sure everything will be fine.

examples.french: J'espère que vous avez passé un bon week-end.
examples.english: I hope you had a good weekend.
examples.note: espérer que keeps the indicative too

blocks.tip: Espérer que is famously indicative in French, even though "to hope" often takes a subjunctive in other Romance languages.

blocks.heading: Negative and question forms: a first taste of doubt
blocks.body: When you deny or question an opinion, the idea is no longer presented as certain, and careful speakers switch to the subjunctive after que. You will study this mood properly in the next lesson; for now, learn the pattern and a few common shapes by heart. In casual spoken French, many people keep the indicative, but the subjunctive is expected in writing and in exams.

examples.french: Je ne pense pas que ce soit une bonne idée.
examples.english: I don't think that's a good idea.

examples.french: Je ne crois pas qu'il ait raison.
examples.english: I don't believe he's right.

examples.french: Penses-tu qu'elle puisse venir ?
examples.english: Do you think she can come?

examples.french: Je ne trouve pas que ce film soit drôle.
examples.english: I don't find this film funny.

examples.french: Je doute qu'il finisse à temps.
examples.english: I doubt he'll finish in time.
examples.note: douter que always takes the subjunctive

blocks.tip: Memorise the three mini-forms now: que ce soit, qu'il ait, qu'il puisse. They cover most conversations.

passages.title: Faut-il fermer la rue aux voitures ?
passages.french:
La mairie propose de fermer la rue principale aux voitures le samedi.
Dans le café du coin, tout le monde en parle.
« À mon avis, c'est une excellente idée », dit Karim, qui habite juste au-dessus.
« Le samedi, on ne s'entend plus parler. Je trouve que le quartier mérite un peu de calme. »
Sa voisine Sylvie est plus prudente.
« Je comprends, mais j'ai l'impression qu'on oublie les commerçants.
Si les clients ne peuvent plus se garer, ils iront ailleurs. »
Karim n'est pas convaincu : « Franchement, les gens viennent surtout à pied. »
« Peut-être », répond Sylvie, « mais je ne suis pas sûre que ce soit vrai pour les personnes âgées. »
Le patron du café, lui, reste mitigé.
« Personnellement, je pense que la mairie devrait d'abord faire un essai pendant trois mois.
Ensuite, on verra bien qui avait raison. »
Tout le monde approuve : au moins sur ce point, ils sont du même avis.
Une réunion publique aura lieu le mois prochain.
passages.english:
The town hall is proposing to close the main street to cars on Saturdays.
In the corner café, everyone is talking about it.
"In my opinion, it's an excellent idea," says Karim, who lives right above.
"On Saturdays, you can't hear yourself speak. I find that the neighborhood deserves a bit of quiet."
His neighbor Sylvie is more cautious.
"I understand, but I get the impression that people are forgetting the shopkeepers.
If customers can't park anymore, they'll go elsewhere."
Karim isn't convinced: "Honestly, people mostly come on foot."
"Maybe," answers Sylvie, "but I'm not sure that's true for elderly people."
The café owner, for his part, has mixed feelings.
"Personally, I think the town hall should first run a three-month trial.
Then we'll see who was right."
Everyone approves: at least on this point, they are of the same opinion.
A public meeting will take place next month.

lessons.title: Il faut que tu saches
lessons.description: Meet the subjunctive: how it is formed and why il faut que and vouloir que demand it.

blocks.heading: What the subjunctive actually does
blocks.body: The subjunctive is not a tense but a mood. The indicative presents facts; the subjunctive presents things filtered through a will, a need, a doubt or an emotion. That is why it almost always appears after que, in a second clause, with a different subject from the first one. English lost most of its subjunctive, so translate the idea, not the form.

examples.french: Il faut que tu partes maintenant.
examples.english: You have to leave now.

examples.french: Je veux que tu me dises la vérité.
examples.english: I want you to tell me the truth.

examples.french: Il est important que nous soyons à l'heure.
examples.english: It's important that we be on time.

examples.french: Elle part maintenant.
examples.english: She is leaving now.

examples.french: Il faut que je fasse les courses ce soir.
examples.english: I have to do the shopping tonight.

examples.french: Mes parents veulent que je rentre avant minuit.
examples.english: My parents want me to come home before midnight.

blocks.tip: Two subjects, one que, a wish or an obligation — that combination is your signal to reach for the subjunctive.

blocks.heading: Building the present subjunctive
blocks.body: For almost every verb, take the ils/elles form of the present indicative, remove -ent, and add -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent. So parler gives ils parlent, stem parl-, and the subjunctive que je parle. The nous and vous forms borrow the endings of the imparfait, which is why they often sound identical to it.

examples.french: ils finissent → que je finisse, que nous finissions
examples.english: they finish → that I finish, that we finish

examples.french: ils attendent → que tu attendes
examples.english: they wait → that you wait

examples.french: Il faut que vous réfléchissiez avant de répondre.
examples.english: You need to think before answering.

examples.french: Je veux que nous parlions calmement.
examples.english: I want us to talk calmly.

examples.french: Il faudrait qu'elle réponde à ce message.
examples.english: She really ought to answer this message.

blocks.tip: For -er verbs, je, tu, il and ils forms sound exactly like the present indicative. Only nous and vous change audibly.

blocks.heading: The irregulars you truly need
blocks.body: A small group of very common verbs has its own subjunctive stem. Learn these six by heart — être, avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, savoir — and you will handle most real conversations. Vouloir (que je veuille) and falloir (qu'il faille) complete the set.

examples.french: Il faut que je sois patient.
examples.english: I have to be patient.
examples.note: être → sois, sois, soit, soyons, soyez, soient

examples.french: Il faut que tu aies ton passeport.
examples.english: You must have your passport.
examples.note: avoir → aie, aies, ait, ayons, ayez, aient

examples.french: Il faut qu'on aille à la banque.
examples.english: We have to go to the bank.
examples.note: aller → aille, ailles, aille, allions, alliez, aillent

examples.french: Il faut que vous fassiez attention.
examples.english: You must be careful.

examples.french: Il faut que tu saches la vérité.

examples.french: Je voudrais qu'il puisse venir avec nous.
examples.english: I'd like him to be able to come with us.

blocks.tip: Say them as chunks — que je sois, que j'aie, que j'aille, que je fasse, que je sache, que je puisse — until they feel automatic.

blocks.heading: Two subjects, or no que at all
blocks.body: The subjunctive needs a change of subject. If the subject stays the same, French drops que and uses an infinitive instead — much simpler, and much more natural. Compare: je veux partir (I want to leave) versus je veux que tu partes (I want you to leave). The same rule applies to il faut, which takes a plain infinitive when nobody in particular is named.

examples.french: Je veux partir tôt.
examples.english: I want to leave early.

examples.french: Je veux que tu partes tôt.
examples.english: I want you to leave early.

examples.french: Il faut réserver à l'avance.
examples.english: One has to book in advance.

examples.french: Il faut que tu réserves à l'avance.

examples.french: Elle préfère rester ici.
examples.english: She prefers to stay here.

examples.french: Elle préfère que nous restions ici.
examples.english: She prefers that we stay here.

blocks.tip: Before you build a subjunctive, ask: is the second subject really different? If not, use the infinitive.

blocks.heading: Conjunctions that always take the subjunctive
blocks.body: Some conjunctions carry the subjunctive automatically, whatever the meaning of the sentence: avant que, jusqu'à ce que, à condition que, à moins que, sans que, pour que, bien que, en attendant que. Learn the conjunction and the mood together, as one package. Note that après que historically takes the indicative — the action there is already real.

examples.french: Je t'appelle avant que tu partes.
examples.english: I'll call you before you leave.

examples.french: Reste ici jusqu'à ce que je sois prêt.
examples.english: Stay here until I'm ready.

examples.french: Je viendrai, à condition que tu sois là.
examples.english: I'll come, provided that you're there.

examples.french: Il est sorti sans que nous le sachions.
examples.english: He went out without us knowing.

examples.french: Je répète pour que tout le monde comprenne.
examples.english: I'm repeating so that everyone understands.

examples.french: Après qu'il est parti, nous avons fermé.
examples.english: After he left, we closed.

blocks.tip: A useful memory hook: everything that happens "not yet, maybe, or on a condition" takes the subjunctive.

passages.title: La veille du départ
passages.french:
— Alors, tout est prêt pour demain ?
— Presque. Il faut encore que je passe à la banque et que je fasse ma valise.
— Attention, il est important que tu aies ton passeport sur toi à l'aéroport.
— Je sais, maman. Il est dans mon sac depuis hier soir.
— Et il faut absolument que tu arrives deux heures avant le vol.
— Deux heures ? Tu exagères un peu, non ?
— Pas du tout. Je préfère que tu attendes à la porte d'embarquement plutôt que de courir dans les couloirs.
— D'accord, d'accord. Je partirai tôt, à condition que le métro fonctionne.
— Prends un taxi, à moins que ton frère puisse t'accompagner.
— Il travaille jusqu'à ce que le magasin ferme, donc ce sera compliqué.
— Bon. Alors promets-moi que tu m'enverras un message dès que tu seras arrivé.
— Promis. Il ne faut pas que tu t'inquiètes, tout ira bien.
— Je sais. C'est normal qu'une mère s'inquiète un peu, quand même.
passages.english:
"So, is everything ready for tomorrow?"
"Almost. I still have to stop by the bank and pack my suitcase."
"Careful, it's important that you have your passport on you at the airport."
"I know, Mum. It's been in my bag since last night."
"And you absolutely have to arrive two hours before the flight."
"Two hours? You're exaggerating a bit, aren't you?"
"Not at all. I'd rather you waited at the boarding gate than ran down the corridors."
"All right, all right. I'll leave early, provided the metro is running."
"Take a taxi, unless your brother can go with you."
"He works until the shop closes, so that will be complicated."
"Fine. Then promise me you'll send me a message as soon as you've arrived."
"I promise. You mustn't worry, everything will be fine."
"I know. It's normal for a mother to worry a little, all the same."

lessons.title: Émotions
lessons.description: Name your feelings and use être + adjective + que + subjunctive to react to what others do.

blocks.heading: Naming what you feel
blocks.body: French usually builds emotions with être + adjective (je suis déçu) or avoir + noun (j'ai peur). The adjective agrees with the person who feels it: content, contente, contents, contentes. Watch out for false friends — être énervé means to be annoyed, not energised.

examples.french: Je suis vraiment ravi de te voir.
examples.english: I'm really delighted to see you.

examples.french: Elle est déçue par les résultats.
examples.english: She is disappointed by the results.

examples.french: Nous sommes un peu inquiets pour lui.
examples.english: We're a little worried about him.

examples.french: Il a honte de sa réaction.
examples.english: He's ashamed of his reaction.

examples.french: J'ai hâte d'être en vacances !
examples.english: I can't wait to be on holiday!

examples.french: Ça m'énerve quand les gens sont en retard.
examples.english: It annoys me when people are late.

blocks.tip: "Je suis excité" does not mean "I'm excited" — say "j'ai hâte" or "je suis impatient" instead.

blocks.heading: Reacting to what someone else does
blocks.body: When you react emotionally to somebody else's action, French uses être + adjective + que + subjunctive. The emotion belongs to you, the action belongs to them, and the subjunctive marks that gap. This is the most useful subjunctive pattern in everyday conversation.

examples.french: Je suis content que tu sois là.
examples.english: I'm happy that you're here.

examples.french: Je suis désolé que vous ayez attendu.
examples.english: I'm sorry you had to wait.

examples.french: Elle est surprise que nous partions déjà.
examples.english: She's surprised that we're leaving already.

examples.french: Nous sommes heureux qu'il puisse venir.
examples.english: We're glad he can come.

examples.french: Je suis triste que tu doives déménager.
examples.english: I'm sad that you have to move away.

examples.french: Il est furieux qu'on ait annulé le concert.
examples.english: He's furious that they cancelled the concert.

blocks.tip: Same subject, no que: "Je suis content d'être là" — happy to be here myself.

blocks.heading: Emotion verbs and impersonal phrases
blocks.body: Verbs of feeling behave the same way: regretter que, avoir peur que, craindre que, s'étonner que and se réjouir que all take the subjunctive. So do impersonal phrases like c'est dommage que and ça me fait plaisir que. In careful writing, avoir peur que and craindre que may add a decorative ne — ne explétif — which carries no negative meaning.

examples.french: Je regrette que tu ne puisses pas venir.
examples.english: I'm sorry you can't come.

examples.french: C'est dommage qu'il pleuve aujourd'hui.
examples.english: It's a shame it's raining today.

examples.french: Ça me fait plaisir que tu penses à moi.
examples.english: It makes me happy that you think of me.

examples.french: J'ai peur qu'il ne soit trop tard.
examples.english: I'm afraid it may be too late.

examples.french: Je me réjouis que le projet avance.
examples.english: I'm delighted that the project is moving forward.

examples.french: Nous nous étonnons qu'elle n'ait rien dit.
examples.english: We're surprised that she said nothing.

blocks.tip: Espérer stays with the indicative even though it feels emotional: j'espère que tu vas bien.

blocks.heading: être + adjective + que + subjunctive
blocks.body: The pattern is fixed: a form of être, an emotion adjective that agrees with the speaker, then que and a subjunctive verb. Adjectives that work this way include content, heureux, ravi, triste, désolé, surpris, étonné, déçu, fier, furieux and gêné. Remember that the adjective agrees with the person feeling the emotion, not with the person acting.

examples.french: Je suis heureuse que tu viennes.
examples.english: I'm happy (f.) that you're coming.

examples.french: Ils sont surpris que nous soyons déjà prêts.
examples.english: They're surprised that we're ready already.

examples.french: Je suis désolé que vous ayez eu ce problème.
examples.english: I'm sorry you had this problem.

examples.french: Elle est fière que son fils fasse du théâtre.
examples.english: She's proud that her son does theatre.

examples.french: Nous sommes déçus qu'il ne vienne pas.
examples.english: We're disappointed that he isn't coming.

blocks.tip: The past subjunctive is easy: avoir or être in the subjunctive + past participle (qu'il ait fini, que tu sois venu).

blocks.heading: Same subject? Use de + infinitive
blocks.body: If the emotion and the action belong to the same person, French avoids que altogether and uses de + infinitive. This is shorter and far more common in speech than the heavy subjunctive version. Compare the pairs below carefully — the meaning changes with the subject, not with the mood.

examples.french: Je suis content d'être ici.
examples.english: I'm happy to be here.

examples.french: Je suis content que tu sois ici.
examples.english: I'm happy that you're here.

examples.french: Elle a peur de se tromper.
examples.english: She's afraid of making a mistake.

examples.french: Elle a peur que nous nous trompions.
examples.english: She's afraid that we'll make a mistake.

examples.french: Nous regrettons de partir si tôt.
examples.english: We're sorry to be leaving so early.

examples.french: Nous regrettons que vous partiez si tôt.
examples.english: We're sorry that you're leaving so early.

blocks.tip: In doubt, ask "who does what?". One person doing both things means de + infinitive.

passages.title: Le message de Léa
passages.french:
Salut Marion,
Je t'écris parce que je n'arrive pas à te joindre au téléphone.
D'abord, je suis vraiment heureuse que tu aies décroché ce stage à Bordeaux.
Je sais à quel point tu y tenais, et je suis fière que tu n'aies jamais lâché.
En même temps, je serais malhonnête si je te disais que tout va bien de mon côté.
Je suis un peu triste que tu partes si loin, même si je comprends parfaitement.
Ces derniers jours, j'ai ressenti une drôle de nostalgie en regardant nos vieilles photos.
Ça m'agace de réagir comme ça, franchement — tu vas à trois heures de train, pas sur la Lune !
J'ai surtout peur qu'on se voie beaucoup moins avec le travail et les horaires.
Mais je me réjouis déjà de venir passer un week-end chez toi cet automne.
En attendant, il faut absolument que tu me racontes ton premier jour.
Je t'appelle dimanche, à moins que tu sois occupée à faire tes cartons.
Je t'embrasse fort,
Léa
passages.english:
Hi Marion,
I'm writing because I can't reach you on the phone.
First of all, I'm really happy that you landed that internship in Bordeaux.
I know how much you wanted it, and I'm proud that you never gave up.
At the same time, I'd be dishonest if I told you everything is fine on my side.
I'm a little sad that you're going so far away, even though I completely understand.
These last few days, I've felt a strange nostalgia looking at our old photos.
It annoys me to react like this, honestly — you're going three hours away by train, not to the Moon!
Mostly I'm afraid we'll see each other much less, with work and schedules.
But I'm already looking forward to coming to spend a weekend at your place this autumn.
In the meantime, you absolutely have to tell me about your first day.
I'll call you on Sunday, unless you're busy packing boxes.
Big hug,
Léa
